domain_restrictions: f is a total function from the Euclidean plane R^2 to the two-element set {red,green}
A,B,C,P,O are points of the Euclidean plane R^2
the hypothesis applies only to triples A,B,C that are noncollinear (hence distinct) so the circumcenter is uniquely defined in R^2
the circumcenter operation circ(A,B,C) is the unique intersection of perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC (uses Euclidean geometry)
root_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every function f: R^2 -> {red,green}, if for all points A,B,C in R^2 that are noncollinear and satisfy f(A)=f(B)=f(C) we have f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A), then there exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c. Equivalently: ∀f [(∀A,B,C (noncollinear ∧ f(A)=f(B)=f(C) ⇒ f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A))) ⇒ (∃c ∈ {red,green} ∀P f(P)=c)].
quantifier_order: forall f : R^2 -> {red,green} (consider any 2-coloring of the plane)
assume (hypothesis) forall A,B,C in R^2: if A,B,C are noncollinear and f(A)=f(B)=f(C) then f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A)
conclude: exists c in {red,green} such that forall P in R^2, f(P) = c

payload.theorem_nl: Suppose that each point in the plane is colored either red or green, subject to the following condition: For every three noncollinear points $A,B,C$ of the same color, the center of the circle passing through $A,B$ and $C$ is also this color. Prove that all points of the plane are the same color.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Given a coloring f satisfying the stated circumcenter condition, select any five points in general position, such as the vertices of a regular pentagon. By the pigeonhole principle, at least three of them have the same color; because no three chosen points are collinear, this yields a monochromatic noncollinear triangle. The hypothesis then implies that the circumcenter O of that triangle has the same color c. Next, no circle centered at O can contain three points of the opposite color, because any such triple would be noncollinear and have circumcenter O, forcing O to have that opposite color as well. Finally, a geometric propagation argument based on equal-radius constructions and the standing hypothesis shows that once every circle centered at O has at most two opposite-colored points, no opposite-colored point can exist anywhere. Hence every point of the plane has color c. Therefore the coloring is constant.

steps.derives: Choose once and for all five distinct points X1,X2,X3,X4,X5 in the plane with no three collinear, for example the vertices of a regular pentagon. Applying L1 to the coloring f and these five points yields indices i<j<k such that Xi,Xj,Xk are noncollinear and have a common color c in {red,green}.
steps.trivial_justification: This step instantiates the finite combinatorial lemma on a concrete 5-point configuration in general position.

steps.derives: Let O = circ(Xi,Xj,Xk). Since Xi,Xj,Xk are noncollinear and all have color c, L2 gives f(O)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: This is a direct application of the circumcenter-preservation hypothesis to the monochromatic noncollinear triple from A1.

steps.derives: For every radius r>0, the circle S(O,r) contains at most two points whose color is different from c.
steps.trivial_justification: L4 applies directly because A2 established that O has color c and f satisfies the standing hypothesis.

steps.derives: For every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: L5 applies with the point O and color c from A2 and with the circle restriction from A3.

steps.derives: There exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: Take the same color c obtained in A1-A2. Step A4 already proves that all points have color c, which is exactly the required existential conclusion.

candidates.strategy_summary: Start by forcing the existence of a monochromatic noncollinear triple via a finite pigeonhole argument on five points in general position. Apply the hypothesis to obtain a monochromatic circumcenter. Then use a circle-centered-at-a-monochromatic-point analysis: any circle centered at such a point can contain at most two points of the opposite color. A final geometric propagation lemma, based on equal-radius circle intersections and 60-degree rotations, upgrades this local circle restriction to global monochromaticity.
